newsitem.title: UK: Firms less confident on UK commercial property.
newsitem.headline: Firms less confident on UK commercial property.

text.p: Confidence in Britain's commercial property market remains positive but less strong than it was six months ago, a survey of businesses revealed on Monday.

"There is less confidence over the next six months than over the last six," Stuart Morley, research head at property consultants Grimley, told a briefing on the Confederation of British Industry (CBI)/Grimley report.

Morley said he was surprised by this result, which did not reflect the strong demand for property experienced on the ground. The caution was likely to have resulted from the British election, which took place mid-way through the survey, he added.
The survey, which covers 564 British firms, found 23 percent expected to increase property holdings, while 22 percent expected to decrease holdings, giving a positive balance of one percent.
This compared with a positive balance of six percent over the previous six months.

Firms in the retail sector saw the largest increases in property holdings over the past six months and are most optimistic about the next six months, with most of the growth likely to come from medium-sized companies.
Energy and water companies were least confident about property holdings and expect to make cutbacks.

"By far the most pessimistic companies are in the water and energy sectors, with the prospect of a windfall tax possibly casting a shadow," Sudhir Junankar, associate director of economic analysis at the CBI, said.
Britain's Labour government, elected on May 1, plans to impose a so-called "windfall tax" on the excess profits made by privatised companies.
Details of the tax and the companies which will pay it are due to be unveiled when Labour announces its first budget on July 2.

Areas showing the strongest growth were Greater London, the rest of South East England and Scotland. South East England and Scotland were expected to see a net increase in property holdings proportionally greater than firms in other regions.
Wales was the only region where an overall net reduction in property holdings was expected.
Expansion was the main reason for increasing capital expenditure on property, Grimley's Morley said, while the main constraint was a shortage of suitable properties.
"The shortage of property is now posing a major constraint and suggests a need for more property development to satisfy demand," he said.

Strong demand and rising rents would lead to an increase in development activity, with the London and South East of England the strongest growth area, followed by the retail sector, warehouses and industrial distribution, Morley said.
Demand for 60 percent of the extra space required by the retail sector was expected to be in town centres, which were where 52 percent of extra office space was likely to be located.
The survey also found business optimism was less buoyant than six months ago, although business output was expected to increase strongly.

Output to the British market would be the major growth market over the next six months, particularly among larger companies and those involved in construction, transport, communications and financial services, the report said.

And an increasing proportion of companies expected profitability to increase over the next six months, while over the last six months 46 percent reported more profitability, with the largest companies making up the largest portion.
The survey also found a more optimistic outlook for employment prospects over the next six months, particularly among smaller companies.
